definition: Pandemonium architecture is a theory in cognitive science that describes how visual images are processed by the brain.
details: It has applications in artificial intelligence and pattern recognition. The theory was introduced by the artificial intelligence pioneer Oliver Selfridge in his 1959 paper "Pandemonium - A Paradigm for Learning". It describes the process of object recognition as the exchange of signals within a hierarchical system of detection and association, the elements of which Selfridge metaphorically termed "demons". This model is now recognized as the basis of visual perception in cognitive science. Pandemonium architecture arose in response to the inability of template matching theories to offer a biologically plausible explanation of the image constancy phenomenon. Contemporary researchers praise this architecture for its elegancy and creativity; that the idea of having multiple independent systems (e.g., feature detectors) working in parallel to address the image constancy phenomena of pattern recognition is powerful yet simple. The basic idea of the pandemonium architecture is that a pattern is first perceived in its parts before the "whole". explainer.lead: Pandemonium architecture is a cognitive science theory of how the brain processes visual images, introduced by Oliver Selfridge in his 1959 paper 'Pandemonium - A Paradigm for Learning'. It matters because it is now recognized as the basis of visual perception in cognitive science and has applications in artificial intelligence and pattern recognition.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a crowd of little workers, each shouting when it spots a feature; the loudest shouts get passed up the line until someone calls out what the object is.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers cite it as an early hierarchical model of object recognition, with detection and association stages exchanging signals. A pitfall is treating the metaphor as a literal algorithm: it is a theory of perception, not a specification.
tiers.paperLevel: Object recognition is described as the exchange of signals within a hierarchical system of detection and association, whose elements Selfridge metaphorically termed 'demons'. It is a conceptual model, so it supplies no formula or error bound.

explainer.example: In the model, low-level 'demons' respond to simple features and pass signals upward to association demons, which together identify the object.
